slides: I want to use the last question to show you four useful arrangements of shapes inside shapes. Each one comes with a fixed ratio. Once we see why, it's worth remembering them.

slides.say: The first one is square, circle, square. A circle inside a square, touching all four sides. And a square inside the circle, with its four corners on the circle. It's exactly the case we just solved.
at: with its four corners on the circle

slides.say: Here the inner square's corners are at the touching points. If it's drawn turned another way, we can rotate it inside the circle until it looks like this. Turning it doesn't change its size. Then the big square is made of eight identical triangles, and the small square of four. So the outer square's area is always twice the inner square's area.
at: the outer square's area is always twice

slides: So when you see this arrangement in a question, you already know the ratio of the areas. The outer area is two times the inner area.

slides.say: It's also worth knowing the sides. Take a radius of one. The outer side is a diameter, two. The inner side is the hypotenuse of a silver triangle with legs one and one, so it's root two. Two is root two times root two. So the outer side is root two times the inner side.
at: The outer side is a diameter
outer side is root two times

slides.say: The second one is circle, square, circle. A square inside a circle, with its four corners on the circle. And a circle inside the square, touching all four sides. It's almost the same case.
at: with its four corners on the circle

slides.say: Why? Say the small radius is one. The small circle touches the square's sides, so the square's side is a diameter, two.
at: Say the small radius is one

slides.say: Now look at the square's diagonal. It cuts the square into two silver triangles with legs of two. In a silver triangle the hypotenuse is the leg times root two. So the diagonal is two root two.
at: Now look at the square's diagonal
So the diagonal is two root two

slides.say: The square's corners are on the big circle, so that diagonal is a diameter of the big circle. So the big radius is half of it, root two.
at: So the big radius is half

slides.say: So the outer radius is root two times the inner radius. Now the areas. The small circle is pi times one squared, which is pi. The big circle is pi times root two squared. Root two squared is two, so that's two pi.

So again, the outer circle's area is exactly twice the inner circle's area. That fits the scaling rule we know. Every length is multiplied by root two. So the area is multiplied by root two squared, which is two.

The third one is triangle, circle, triangle. Here both triangles must be equilateral. A circle inside the big triangle, touching all three sides. And a small triangle inside the circle, with its three corners on the circle.
at: with its three corners on the circle

slides.say: Here it's different. The outer triangle's area isn't twice the inner one. It's four times the inner area. And the outer side is twice the inner side.

Why? The circle touches each side of the big triangle right in its middle, because the equilateral triangle is symmetric. The small triangle in this picture is already turned upside down. If it's drawn another way, we can rotate it around the center until it looks like this. Turning it doesn't change its size. Now its corners touch those middles.
So the big triangle is cut into four equal triangles, and the small one is one of them. Its side is half of the big side, and its area is a quarter. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
